ISO {0} is the international standard for container identification. It sets the owner code, the equipment category letter, the six-digit serial number, the check digit and the size and type code.
How is the check digit worked out?
What does the fourth letter mean?

It is the equipment category. U is a freight container, J is detachable freight-container related equipment such as a generator set, and Z is a trailer or chassis. Almost every container you handle ends its prefix in U.
The check digit is wrong. What now?
Does a valid check digit mean the container exists?
No. It only means the number is correctly formed. Only the shipping line or the container owner can tell you if that box is real and which booking it belongs to.

Who pays, and who carries the risk.
Blue steps are paid by the seller, yellow steps by the buyer. Costs move to the buyer at a different point under each rule.
The red line shows the moment loss or damage stops being the seller’s problem. Under C rules this is long before the cost split.
Export clearance sits with the seller under every rule except EXW. Import clearance sits with the buyer under every rule except DDP.
EXW, FCA, CPT, CIP, DAP, DPU and DDP work for air, road, rail, sea and multimodal moves, including containers. FCA, CPT and CIP are the right choice for most containerised and air cargo.
FAS, FOB, CFR and CIF are built around a ship’s rail. They suit bulk and breakbulk cargo. With containers, the box is handed over at a terminal days before loading, so FCA, CPT or CIP fit better.
Which Incoterm is best for exporters from India?
What is the difference between FOB and FCA?

Under FOB the risk passes when the goods are on board the ship, which suits bulk cargo. Under FCA it passes when the goods are handed to the buyer’s carrier, for example at a CFS or ICD, which is what really happens with containers and air cargo.
Do Incoterms decide when ownership passes?
Does CIF give the buyer full insurance?
Not necessarily. CIF only requires minimum cover, Institute Cargo Clauses (C). Buyers who want all-risks cover should ask for it in the contract or buy extra cover. CIP requires all-risks cover.

The lithium battery rules in plain words

Lithium ion cells up to {0} Wh and batteries up to {1} Wh, or lithium metal cells up to {2} g and batteries up to {3} g, can use the lighter Section II rules within the quantity limits. Anything bigger is fully regulated Class {4}.
Lithium ion batteries shipped on their own must be at {0}% charge or less. From {1}, lithium ion batteries above {2} Wh packed with equipment must also be at {3}% or less.
UN{0} and UN{1}, batteries shipped without equipment, are forbidden on passenger aircraft. They must fly on freighters and carry the Cargo Aircraft Only label.
What is the difference between UN{0} and UN{1}?

UN{0} is lithium ion batteries shipped on their own. UN{1} is lithium ion batteries packed with equipment (PI {2}) or contained in equipment (PI {3}), such as phones and laptops. UN{4} and UN{5} are the lithium metal equivalents.
Multiply the capacity in ampere-hours by the nominal voltage: Wh = mAh ÷ {0} × V. A {1} mAh phone battery at {2} V is {3} Wh, so it is within the {4} Wh Section II limit.
Do Section II lithium batteries need a dangerous goods declaration?

No. Section II shipments do not need a Shipper’s Declaration, but they still need the lithium battery mark (with some exceptions for equipment), a statement on the air waybill and a UN {0} test summary.
What is a UN {0} test summary?

Every lithium cell and battery type must pass the UN {0} tests for altitude, temperature, vibration, shock, short circuit and overcharge. Manufacturers must provide a test summary, and airlines and customs can ask for it.
Can I ship mobile phones by air from India?

Yes. Phones with batteries inside are UN{0} under PI {1}, usually Section II. YAM is Mumbai airport’s #{2} customs broker for mobile phone exports and handles the paperwork, labels and airline acceptance every day.
Are courier and passenger rules the same?
No. This checker covers air cargo under the IATA Dangerous Goods Regulations. Courier companies and passenger baggage have their own, often stricter, rules.

How much cargo really fits in a container?

India's export incentives in plain words

Refunds embedded taxes not refunded elsewhere, like fuel VAT, mandi tax and electricity duty. Rates per {0}-digit HS code in Appendix {1}R (regular exporters) and {2}RE (AA, EOU and SEZ). Credited as a transferable e-scrip.
Most goods are Free to export. Some are Restricted (need a DGFT licence), Prohibited, or allowed only through a state trading enterprise. Check before you sell.
What is the difference between drawback and RoDTEP?

Duty drawback refunds customs duty and central excise paid on inputs used to make the export product. RoDTEP refunds other taxes and levies that are not refunded anywhere else, such as VAT on fuel, mandi tax and electricity duty. They cover different taxes, so you can claim both on the same shipment.

Can AA, EOU and SEZ exporters get RoDTEP?

Yes. Since {0}, exports by Advance Authorisation holders, EOUs and SEZ units get RoDTEP at the Appendix {1}RE rates, which are lower than the Appendix {2}R rates for regular exporters. They cannot claim All Industry Rate drawback.
Why do I have to pick a drawback line?

The drawback schedule follows the Customs Tariff only at the {0}-digit heading. Below that it has its own sub-items, for example by fibre for garments. Pick the line that describes your goods; we pre-select our best match.

Your customs broker claims them on the shipping bill. Drawback is paid into your bank account after the export is completed. RoDTEP and RoSCTL are issued as transferable e-scrips on ICEGATE, which you can use to pay import duty or sell to other importers.

What is the difference between HAZ, DG and general cargo?

HAZ (hazardous) and DG (dangerous goods) mean the same thing in shipping: goods with a UN number under the IMDG Code (sea) or the IATA / ICAO rules (air). General cargo is anything that is not DG. Some general cargo still needs special handling, such as perishables, valuables or out-of-gauge cargo.

What does the fourth letter mean?

It is the equipment category. U is a freight container, J is detachable freight-container related equipment such as a generator set, and Z is a trailer or chassis. Almost every container you handle ends its prefix in U.
The check digit is wrong. What now?

Most often it is a typo or a misread character, such as O for {0} or I for {1}. Check the number on the container door and on the booking or bill of lading. If it still fails, ask the shipping line before you file the document.
Does a valid check digit mean the container exists?

Incoterms® are trade rules published by the International Chamber of Commerce. A three-letter code such as FOB or DAP in your sales contract decides who pays for each part of the journey, who handles customs, and when the risk of loss passes from seller to buyer.
Which Incoterm is best for exporters from India?

For containers and air cargo, FCA or CPT/CIP usually work best: you clear the goods for export, keep control of your shipping bill for GST refunds, RoDTEP and drawback, and hand over at a clear point. Avoid EXW for exports.
What is the difference between FOB and FCA?

Under FOB the risk passes when the goods are on board the ship, which suits bulk cargo. Under FCA it passes when the goods are handed to the buyer’s carrier, for example at a CFS or ICD, which is what really happens with containers and air cargo.
Do Incoterms decide when ownership passes?
No. Incoterms cover costs, risk and customs duties. Transfer of ownership, payment terms and the price are agreed separately in the sales contract and the letter of credit.
Does CIF give the buyer full insurance?
Not necessarily. CIF only requires minimum cover, Institute Cargo Clauses (C). Buyers who want all-risks cover should ask for it in the contract or buy extra cover. CIP requires all-risks cover.

How is Indian import duty calculated?

Basic customs duty (BCD) is charged on the assessable value, which is the CIF value converted at the CBIC customs exchange rate. Landing charges (the old {0}%) have not been added since CBIC amended the valuation rules in {1}. If freight or insurance is not known, customs practice is to add {2}% of the FOB value for freight and {3}% for insurance. Social welfare surcharge (SWS) is normally {4}% of the BCD. IGST is then charged on the assessable value plus BCD and SWS. Some goods also attract agriculture cess (AIDC), compensation cess, anti-dumping or safeguard duty.

What does Restricted or Prohibited mean?

Restricted goods need an import authorisation or must meet a DGFT policy condition, such as a licence, registration or certificate. Prohibited goods cannot be imported. State trading (STE) goods can only be imported through notified state agencies.
Do trade agreements reduce the duty?

Often, yes. Goods that qualify under the rules of origin of an agreement such as India–UAE CEPA, India–ASEAN or India–Japan CEPA can pay lower or zero basic customs duty, with a valid certificate of origin. IGST is still payable.

Does the HSN code tell me if my cargo is dangerous goods?

Not on its own. HSN is a customs tariff code; dangerous goods are classified by the substance and its properties, shown as a UN number in Section {0} of the MSDS. The same HSN heading can hold both DG and non-DG products, which is why this checker gives a likelihood and tells you what to check.
What is the difference between HAZ, DG and general cargo?

HAZ (hazardous) and DG (dangerous goods) mean the same thing in shipping: goods with a UN number under the IMDG Code (sea) or the IATA / ICAO rules (air). General cargo is anything that is not DG. Some general cargo still needs special handling, such as perishables, valuables or out-of-gauge cargo.

In Section {0} (Transport information) of the product’s Safety Data Sheet (MSDS / SDS). If Section {1} says “not regulated” or “not dangerous goods”, the product is normally shipped as general cargo.

Lines, CFSs and airlines check chemicals, oils, powders and similar cargo to make sure nothing dangerous is misdeclared. Misdeclared cargo has caused serious ship fires, so most lines want the MSDS and a non-hazardous declaration on your letterhead.

Who pays, and who carries the risk.
Blue steps are paid by the seller, yellow steps by the buyer. Costs move to the buyer at a different point under each rule.
The red line shows the moment loss or damage stops being the seller’s problem. Under C rules this is long before the cost split.
Export clearance sits with the seller under every rule except EXW. Import clearance sits with the buyer under every rule except DDP.
EXW, FCA, CPT, CIP, DAP, DPU and DDP work for air, road, rail, sea and multimodal moves, including containers. FCA, CPT and CIP are the right choice for most containerised and air cargo.
FAS, FOB, CFR and CIF are built around a ship’s rail. They suit bulk and breakbulk cargo. With containers, the box is handed over at a terminal days before loading, so FCA, CPT or CIP fit better.

What is the difference between FOB and FCA?

Under FOB the risk passes when the goods are on board the ship, which suits bulk cargo. Under FCA it passes when the goods are handed to the buyer’s carrier, for example at a CFS or ICD, which is what really happens with containers and air cargo.

Does CIF give the buyer full insurance?
Not necessarily. CIF only requires minimum cover, Institute Cargo Clauses (C). Buyers who want all-risks cover should ask for it in the contract or buy extra cover. CIP requires all-risks cover.

What is the difference between HAZ, DG and general cargo?

HAZ (hazardous) and DG (dangerous goods) mean the same thing in shipping: goods with a UN number under the IMDG Code (sea) or the IATA / ICAO rules (air). General cargo is anything that is not DG. Some general cargo still needs special handling, such as perishables, valuables or out-of-gauge cargo.

Who pays, and who carries the risk.
Blue steps are paid by the seller, yellow steps by the buyer. Costs move to the buyer at a different point under each rule.
The red line shows the moment loss or damage stops being the seller’s problem. Under C rules this is long before the cost split.
Export clearance sits with the seller under every rule except EXW. Import clearance sits with the buyer under every rule except DDP.
EXW, FCA, CPT, CIP, DAP, DPU and DDP work for air, road, rail, sea and multimodal moves, including containers. FCA, CPT and CIP are the right choice for most containerised and air cargo.
FAS, FOB, CFR and CIF are built around a ship’s rail. They suit bulk and breakbulk cargo. With containers, the box is handed over at a terminal days before loading, so FCA, CPT or CIP fit better.

What is the difference between FOB and FCA?

Under FOB the risk passes when the goods are on board the ship, which suits bulk cargo. Under FCA it passes when the goods are handed to the buyer’s carrier, for example at a CFS or ICD, which is what really happens with containers and air cargo.
Do Incoterms decide when ownership passes?
Does CIF give the buyer full insurance?
Not necessarily. CIF only requires minimum cover, Institute Cargo Clauses (C). Buyers who want all-risks cover should ask for it in the contract or buy extra cover. CIP requires all-risks cover.

What is the difference between FOB and FCA?

Under FOB the risk passes when the goods are on board the ship, which suits bulk cargo. Under FCA it passes when the goods are handed to the buyer’s carrier, for example at a CFS or ICD, which is what really happens with containers and air cargo.

Does CIF give the buyer full insurance?
Not necessarily. CIF only requires minimum cover, Institute Cargo Clauses (C). Buyers who want all-risks cover should ask for it in the contract or buy extra cover. CIP requires all-risks cover.

What is the difference between HAZ, DG and general cargo?

HAZ (hazardous) and DG (dangerous goods) mean the same thing in shipping: goods with a UN number under the IMDG Code (sea) or the IATA / ICAO rules (air). General cargo is anything that is not DG. Some general cargo still needs special handling, such as perishables, valuables or out-of-gauge cargo.

Why do shipping lines ask for an MSDS even for non-DG cargo?

Lines, CFSs and airlines check chemicals, oils, powders and similar cargo to make sure nothing dangerous is misdeclared. Misdeclared cargo has caused serious ship fires, so most lines want the MSDS and a non-hazardous declaration on your letterhead.

Who pays, and who carries the risk.
Blue steps are paid by the seller, yellow steps by the buyer. Costs move to the buyer at a different point under each rule.
The red line shows the moment loss or damage stops being the seller’s problem. Under C rules this is long before the cost split.
Export clearance sits with the seller under every rule except EXW. Import clearance sits with the buyer under every rule except DDP.
EXW, FCA, CPT, CIP, DAP, DPU and DDP work for air, road, rail, sea and multimodal moves, including containers. FCA, CPT and CIP are the right choice for most containerised and air cargo.
FAS, FOB, CFR and CIF are built around a ship’s rail. They suit bulk and breakbulk cargo. With containers, the box is handed over at a terminal days before loading, so FCA, CPT or CIP fit better.

What is the difference between FOB and FCA?

Under FOB the risk passes when the goods are on board the ship, which suits bulk cargo. Under FCA it passes when the goods are handed to the buyer’s carrier, for example at a CFS or ICD, which is what really happens with containers and air cargo.
Do Incoterms decide when ownership passes?
Does CIF give the buyer full insurance?
Not necessarily. CIF only requires minimum cover, Institute Cargo Clauses (C). Buyers who want all-risks cover should ask for it in the contract or buy extra cover. CIP requires all-risks cover.

What is the difference between HAZ, DG and general cargo?

HAZ (hazardous) and DG (dangerous goods) mean the same thing in shipping: goods with a UN number under the IMDG Code (sea) or the IATA / ICAO rules (air). General cargo is anything that is not DG. Some general cargo still needs special handling, such as perishables, valuables or out-of-gauge cargo.

Why do shipping lines ask for an MSDS even for non-DG cargo?

Lines, CFSs and airlines check chemicals, oils, powders and similar cargo to make sure nothing dangerous is misdeclared. Misdeclared cargo has caused serious ship fires, so most lines want the MSDS and a non-hazardous declaration on your letterhead.

Who pays, and who carries the risk.
Blue steps are paid by the seller, yellow steps by the buyer. Costs move to the buyer at a different point under each rule.
The red line shows the moment loss or damage stops being the seller’s problem. Under C rules this is long before the cost split.
Export clearance sits with the seller under every rule except EXW. Import clearance sits with the buyer under every rule except DDP.
EXW, FCA, CPT, CIP, DAP, DPU and DDP work for air, road, rail, sea and multimodal moves, including containers. FCA, CPT and CIP are the right choice for most containerised and air cargo.
FAS, FOB, CFR and CIF are built around a ship’s rail. They suit bulk and breakbulk cargo. With containers, the box is handed over at a terminal days before loading, so FCA, CPT or CIP fit better.

What is the difference between FOB and FCA?

Under FOB the risk passes when the goods are on board the ship, which suits bulk cargo. Under FCA it passes when the goods are handed to the buyer’s carrier, for example at a CFS or ICD, which is what really happens with containers and air cargo.
Do Incoterms decide when ownership passes?
Does CIF give the buyer full insurance?
Not necessarily. CIF only requires minimum cover, Institute Cargo Clauses (C). Buyers who want all-risks cover should ask for it in the contract or buy extra cover. CIP requires all-risks cover.

What is the difference between HAZ, DG and general cargo?

HAZ (hazardous) and DG (dangerous goods) mean the same thing in shipping: goods with a UN number under the IMDG Code (sea) or the IATA / ICAO rules (air). General cargo is anything that is not DG. Some general cargo still needs special handling, such as perishables, valuables or out-of-gauge cargo.

Why do shipping lines ask for an MSDS even for non-DG cargo?

Lines, CFSs and airlines check chemicals, oils, powders and similar cargo to make sure nothing dangerous is misdeclared. Misdeclared cargo has caused serious ship fires, so most lines want the MSDS and a non-hazardous declaration on your letterhead.

What is the difference between HAZ, DG and general cargo?

HAZ (hazardous) and DG (dangerous goods) mean the same thing in shipping: goods with a UN number under the IMDG Code (sea) or the IATA / ICAO rules (air). General cargo is anything that is not DG. Some general cargo still needs special handling, such as perishables, valuables or out-of-gauge cargo.

Lines, CFSs and airlines check chemicals, oils, powders and similar cargo to make sure nothing dangerous is misdeclared. Misdeclared cargo has caused serious ship fires, so most lines want the MSDS and a non-hazardous declaration on your letterhead.

Who pays, and who carries the risk.
Blue steps are paid by the seller, yellow steps by the buyer. Costs move to the buyer at a different point under each rule.
The red line shows the moment loss or damage stops being the seller’s problem. Under C rules this is long before the cost split.
Export clearance sits with the seller under every rule except EXW. Import clearance sits with the buyer under every rule except DDP.
EXW, FCA, CPT, CIP, DAP, DPU and DDP work for air, road, rail, sea and multimodal moves, including containers. FCA, CPT and CIP are the right choice for most containerised and air cargo.
FAS, FOB, CFR and CIF are built around a ship’s rail. They suit bulk and breakbulk cargo. With containers, the box is handed over at a terminal days before loading, so FCA, CPT or CIP fit better.
Which Incoterm is best for exporters from India?
What is the difference between FOB and FCA?

Under FOB the risk passes when the goods are on board the ship, which suits bulk cargo. Under FCA it passes when the goods are handed to the buyer’s carrier, for example at a CFS or ICD, which is what really happens with containers and air cargo.
Do Incoterms decide when ownership passes?
Does CIF give the buyer full insurance?
Not necessarily. CIF only requires minimum cover, Institute Cargo Clauses (C). Buyers who want all-risks cover should ask for it in the contract or buy extra cover. CIP requires all-risks cover.

HAZ (hazardous) and DG (dangerous goods) mean the same thing in shipping: goods with a UN number under the IMDG Code (sea) or the IATA / ICAO rules (air). General cargo is anything that is not DG. Some general cargo still needs special handling, such as perishables, valuables or out-of-gauge cargo.

Who pays, and who carries the risk.
Blue steps are paid by the seller, yellow steps by the buyer. Costs move to the buyer at a different point under each rule.
The red line shows the moment loss or damage stops being the seller’s problem. Under C rules this is long before the cost split.
Export clearance sits with the seller under every rule except EXW. Import clearance sits with the buyer under every rule except DDP.
EXW, FCA, CPT, CIP, DAP, DPU and DDP work for air, road, rail, sea and multimodal moves, including containers. FCA, CPT and CIP are the right choice for most containerised and air cargo.
FAS, FOB, CFR and CIF are built around a ship’s rail. They suit bulk and breakbulk cargo. With containers, the box is handed over at a terminal days before loading, so FCA, CPT or CIP fit better.

What is the difference between FOB and FCA?

Under FOB the risk passes when the goods are on board the ship, which suits bulk cargo. Under FCA it passes when the goods are handed to the buyer’s carrier, for example at a CFS or ICD, which is what really happens with containers and air cargo.
Do Incoterms decide when ownership passes?
Does CIF give the buyer full insurance?
Not necessarily. CIF only requires minimum cover, Institute Cargo Clauses (C). Buyers who want all-risks cover should ask for it in the contract or buy extra cover. CIP requires all-risks cover.

FAS, FOB, CFR and CIF are built around a ship’s rail. They suit bulk and breakbulk cargo. With containers, the box is handed over at a terminal days before loading, so FCA, CPT or CIP fit better.

What is the difference between FOB and FCA?

Under FOB the risk passes when the goods are on board the ship, which suits bulk cargo. Under FCA it passes when the goods are handed to the buyer’s carrier, for example at a CFS or ICD, which is what really happens with containers and air cargo.

Does CIF give the buyer full insurance?
Not necessarily. CIF only requires minimum cover, Institute Cargo Clauses (C). Buyers who want all-risks cover should ask for it in the contract or buy extra cover. CIP requires all-risks cover.

Does the HSN code tell me if my cargo is dangerous goods?
What is the difference between HAZ, DG and general cargo?

HAZ (hazardous) and DG (dangerous goods) mean the same thing in shipping: goods with a UN number under the IMDG Code (sea) or the IATA / ICAO rules (air). General cargo is anything that is not DG. Some general cargo still needs special handling, such as perishables, valuables or out-of-gauge cargo.

Why do shipping lines ask for an MSDS even for non-DG cargo?

Lines, CFSs and airlines check chemicals, oils, powders and similar cargo to make sure nothing dangerous is misdeclared. Misdeclared cargo has caused serious ship fires, so most lines want the MSDS and a non-hazardous declaration on your letterhead.
